  PLANS AND PRIORITY INITIATIVE ACTION PLANS

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

    Engaged and Connected Residents
    Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Services
    Fiscally Responsible and Transparent City Government

BACKGROUND

As we have worked together to develop an innovative budget process for FY20, the City Council and the
Budget Subcommittee (Council Members Jakubowski and Ude) indicated that a helpful first step would
be an understanding of current year activities, including the development of departmental operational
plans to clearly define each program the department manages and the associated activities and operating
metrics.

Today’s discussion will include a presentation of the full operational plans developed by each department,
as well as a higher-level overview of the priority initiative action plans that are currently being developed
in Envisio, our new strategic planning and performance management software.

As a reminder, “Operational Plans” reflect the work that each department does on a daily basis. These are
the programs that are continuously managed by each department, year in and year out. These are generally
static and do not change, unless a budget reduction is directed that requires the elimination of program
areas. In other words, Operational Plans represent a department’s normal business. On the other hand,
“Priority Initiative Action Plans” reflect the special projects that a department might take on in a given
year – these are generally either one-time only or new initiatives. These projects take extra resources and
must be accomplished while still maintaining the department’s normal course of business. Some priority
initiatives will simply be completed and fall off the list, while others will be launched and then become
part of the department’s normal operating business. As an example of the former, the website redesign,
once completed, will fall of the list – it is a one-time project. As an example of the latter, launching a

social media presence will occur once . . . but then the maintenance of that social media presence will shift
to the Operational Plan because it will now be part of my department’s normal course of business.

DISCUSSION

On November 30, 2018, City Council received a “preview” of the template for department operational
plans. This template had already been reviewed by members of the Budget Subcommittee on November
19, who were pleased with the template and gave only minor formatting edits that were then incorporated.

To ensure the department operational plans meet the needs of City Council, the Executive Team met with
the Budget Subcommittee again on December 20 to present and discuss the completed operational plan
manual. Council Members Jakubowski and Ude were each given a copy of the manual to review and
received one sample presentation. Council Members Jakubowski and Ude were impressed with the manual
and provided no additional edits to the format.

Simultaneously, staff has also been working to create action plans for all priority initiatives for input into
the Envisio software. Again, unlike the operational plans, which explain the regular, day-to-day operations
and activities of each department, priority initiatives are typically Council-driven, time-bound projects
that came out of the strategic planning process or other Council direction. While the Envisio software is
currently in the development phase, we were able to produce simplified summary reports to show City
Council what actions are being taken by staff to successfully implement all priority initiatives. Once
Envisio is fully implemented, the reports will be more graphic-based and show clear progress updates for
each priority initiative.

Together, the operational plans and priority initiative action plans capture the work being done by each
department this year.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council hear presentations from each department on their Operational
Plans and Priority Initiative Action Plans, and accept the manual.

  3. ACTIVITIES - METHODS OF ENFORCEMENT
  a. Verbal Warning- An observed or reported code violation is immediately resolved as a
  result of a conversation- in person or on phone. Compliance inspection conducted.
  b. Courtesy Notice- An observed or reported code violation does not meet the criteria
  to be a violation but could as a result of no actions.
  c. 1st Notice of Violation- An observed or reported code violation clearly meets the
  criteria to be a violation and action is required.
  d. 2nd Notice of Violation- A follow-up compliance inspection confirms that the
  observed or reported code violation has not been completely resolved in a timely
  manner.
  e. Final Notice of Violation- A follow-up compliance inspection confirms that the
  observed or reported code violation remains unresolved and full compliance has not
  achieved in a timely manner.
  f. Notice of Recurring Violation- A previous observed or reported code violation that
  was deemed compliant has been re-inspected and a repeat violation has been
  confirmed.
  g. Administrative Citations- Specific violations to code section 01.06.01 may result in an
  administrative citation(s) being administered. First violation by a fine not exceeding
  one hundred dollars ($100.00), and for committing the same offense a second time
  within one year, by a fine not exceeding two hundred dollars ($200.00) and for
  committing the same offense a third or any subsequent time within one year, by a
  fine not exceeding five hundred dollars ($500.00)
  h. Declaration of Public Nuisance-Public Nuisance proceedings include a notice of
  violation sent via certified mail. If violation is not abated within the specified time
  frame, the item is set for hearing before the Planning Commission.
